source: Wisconsin Administrative Code chapter NR 40 (Invasive Species Identification, Classification and Control), Register November 2024 No. 827

plants.why: It spreads fast through forests and puts chemicals in the soil that hurt native plants and young trees.
It grows into thick thickets that stay green late into fall and shade out wildflowers and young trees.
It forms thick thickets in wetlands and woods that crowd out native plants.
One plant can make millions of seeds, and it chokes the wetlands that ducks, frogs, and turtles need.
It takes over roadsides and prairies, and its sap can burn skin when the sun hits it.
plants.warning: Don't touch! The sap can cause painful burns and blisters in sunlight.

plants.why: It grows so strong it can push up through pavement, and its thick patches crowd out plants along rivers.
This bush honeysuckle leafs out early in spring and shades out the wildflowers below it.
This bush honeysuckle forms dense shrubs that crowd out native plants in woods and fields.
This bush honeysuckle spreads when birds eat its berries, and it shades out plants on the forest floor.
This tall bush honeysuckle grows into thick walls of shrubs that block sunlight from everything underneath.
It takes over sunny, dry places like prairies and makes it hard for other plants to grow nearby.
Its very deep roots make it almost impossible to pull out, and its milky sap can irritate skin.
This vine wraps tightly around trees and can strangle them or pull them down.
It grows very fast, sends up new sprouts from its roots, and is a favorite food of the spotted lanternfly pest.
It grows into huge thorny thickets that people and animals can't get through.
It looks like a pretty wildflower, but it spreads into woods and crowds out native flowers.
Birds spread its berries everywhere, and it changes the soil in ways that help it crowd out prairie plants.
Its roots creep underground and pop up as big prickly patches that crowd out other plants.
Its big flat leaves smother the plants underneath, and it spreads from roadsides into prairies.
It forms thorny thickets that deer won't eat, and those thickets can be good homes for ticks.
This vine smothers other plants and tricks monarch butterflies into laying eggs where caterpillars can't survive.
Every part of this plant is very poisonous to people and animals.
plants.warning: Don't touch it and never eat it! Every part is very poisonous.

plants.why: The non-native kind grows in tall, thick walls that take over wetlands, but a native kind looks similar, so experts need to check.
This giant plant crowds out others, and its sap can cause bad burns on skin in sunlight.
plants.warning: Don't touch! The sap can cause serious burns and blisters in sunlight.

plants.why: This vine grows super fast and can cover and smother whole trees.
This prickly vine grows very fast and smothers other plants under a blanket of leaves.
It spreads quickly across forest floors and crowds out wildflowers and baby trees.
This vine climbs over shrubs and small trees and blocks their sunlight.
It grows taller than a basketball hoop in thick patches that crowd out plants along rivers.
It carpets the forest floor in spring and crowds out native spring wildflowers.
